dotplot.name: dotplot
dotplot.note: this looks more sparse than expected to me. not sure if we are using different dataset or if its regressed, i want the full size paf not the small one. DONE 2026-08-08, and the answer is neither a different dataset nor a regression. IT WAS ALREADY THE FULL PAF -- the spec loads the hosted peach_grape.paf.gz rather than the small in-repo one the config's defaultSession uses. What made it sparse was the spec's own minAlignmentLength: 2000, which was discarding 87% of it. Measured off the file: 16,192 records, median block 675 bp, p90 2,287 bp, longest 11,450 bp, so a 2 kb floor keeps 2,126 blocks and a 1 kb floor keeps 5,983. The filter is gone. The old comment justified it on the grounds that every block is sub-pixel against a 227 x 486 Mbp plot so the filter 'is what leaves anything readable', which has it backwards for a dotplot: a sub-pixel block IS a dot, and the structure is the density of dots along a diagonal, so thinning them thins the signal. Rendered all three (2000, 1000, 0) and compared rather than reasoning about it: the diagonals across grape chr5/chr9/chr17 and the Pp03 and Pp06 columns are faint streaks at 2000 and continuous runs at 0. Worth knowing for the caption if you want it there: the horizontal bands on grape chr12-chr14 are repeat-driven hits spread across every peach chromosome, they are present at every threshold, and they are proportionally LEAST dominant unfiltered.

sv_cgiab/cnv_with_bed_track.note: BAF added, and the coverage lane fixed so it can be read. Both halves of the note. (1) THE BAF TRACK: chr5 is the chromosome that most rewards one -- the benchmark calls three allelic states on it where chr3 (cnv_depth_baf) has two. Measured off the hosted bigWig per 2 Mb of het sites: chr5:20-22 Mb CN 2 (1|1) is 84% between 0.4 and 0.6, chr5:37-39 Mb CN 3 (2|1) is 45% at 0.15-0.4 and 49% at 0.6-0.85, chr5:60-62 Mb CN 1 (0|1) is 48% below 0.15 and 51% above 0.85 with nothing between. So the lane draws one band, then the 1/3-2/3 fork the tutorial's own table predicts for a gain, then the two LOH bands. (2) NORMALIZED READ DEPTH, and the tool that does it: that is what the coverage lane already was -- goleft indexcov normalizes each sample to its own median, which is the only reason the two rows can be read against each other. It did not LOOK like it because the display was on localsd autoscale while the walkthrough text tells the reader to apply a manual min/max cap: indexcov's centromere and repeat spikes run to 497, so every plateau sat in the bottom fifth of the lane as one cloud. The complaint was right and the diagnosis was that it reads as random RGB — which it literally was: the hash mapped straight into HSL, whose hue wheel spends a quarter of itself on greens that look identical and a sliver on yellow, and which at one nominal lightness gives glaring yellows beside murky blues. That unevenness is the whole difference between a hash palette and a curated one. It now places the same hash's hue in OKLCH at a fixed lightness and chroma (three tiers, 0.56/0.66/0.75 L), gamut-mapped by reducing chroma at constant hue rather than by clipping a channel, and returns hex. Every value now comes out equally light and equally colorful, which is the property Tableau10/Okabe-Ito actually have. In this figure the six named orthologs went from electric magenta / acid yellow-green / navy / dark crimson to a coherent set (soft blue, warm brown, light blue, green, purple, pink). It stays a hash rather than a list of N curated colors, and that part of the earlier answer still holds: randomColor has no shared state, so there is no allocator handing out the next unused color, and an N-colour palette repeats after N values and collides by the birthday problem long before — six values into a twenty-colour palette collide more often than not. A hue circle does not repeat until 360. Tests rewritten around what the change actually asserts: lightness and chroma inside the categorical band, and 500 distinct inputs producing >300 distinct colors, which a fixed palette cannot.
